stances.claim: There is no fire in the popular belly for federalism -- Duterte's own lament is validated by surveys showing the masses don't understand or support it.
stances.rhetorical_move: president's own words as indictment of the federalism rollout

stances.claim: The 1987 Constitution is good but not perfect and needs updating -- specifically its ultranationalistic provisions overtaken by 21st-century technology and globalization.
Globalization should be explained to the masses not in economic legalese but as what OFWs and BPO workers experience: better-paying jobs that put food on the table.
Federalism must be explained in easy-to-understand terms -- using the medical analogy (symptoms, tests, diagnosis, remedies) and the car analogy (check battery before ordering an overhaul).
Only use extreme, disruptive, or risky remedies (heart transplant, engine overhaul) if absolutely needed -- know the root cause before rushing to the solution.
stances.rhetorical_move: proportionality-of-remedy principle as the column's closing lesson

notable_anecdotes: Duterte lamenting publicly that the masses do not understand and support federalism -- the proponent-in-chief conceding the communication failure.

The medical analogy: a patient with chest pains needs symptoms → tests (ECG, echocardiogram, stress test, MRI, angiography) → diagnosis → remedy (meds, angioplasty, bypass surgery, or transplant) -- don't order a transplant before diagnosing.
The car analogy: if the car won't start, check the battery and electrical wires first before ordering an engine overhaul.

Globalization explained at the kitchen-table level: OFWs obtaining better-paying jobs abroad; BPO workers earning foreign-country wages locally -- these put food on tables, buy TV sets, and build better houses.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reports that Duterte himself has lamented the masses don't understand or support federalism -- a lament validated by surveys -- and attributes this to federalism proponents' confusing and conflicting concepts and theories. Building on his January 7 column, he reaffirms he is not convinced on federalism but is open to listening once the specifics are clear. He concedes the 1987 Constitution needs updating -- particularly its ultranationalistic provisions overtaken by 21st-century technology (internet, smartphones) and globalization (OFW remittances and BPO wages as the economy's main drivers) -- and proposes those changes be explained not in economists' legalese ('free flow of goods and services in a borderless world') but in the language of what OFWs and BPO workers actually experience ('obtaining better-paying jobs that put food on the table'). The core prescription is analogical: explaining federalism should follow the diagnostic process of medicine -- know the symptoms, run the tests, establish the diagnosis and root cause, then consider remedies from mild (medication) to extreme (heart transplant), recognizing that 'risks of heart transplants are far worse than bypass surgery'; or like a car that won't start -- check the battery before ordering an engine overhaul. The column's closing principle: know the root cause before rushing to the solution, and only use extreme, disruptive, or risky remedies -- comparable to heart transplants and engine overhauls -- if absolutely necessary.
